algorithm.Title: Abdomen Bloating and Swelling - Female (Child)
algorithm.ContentSet: IST Open-Source Guideline Content | Child | Female
Definition: UAT-only assessment of abdominal bloating or swelling across adult and pediatric patients; not approved for real-patient or production use.

Background.ExpertReviewer: Pending qualified Qatar adult, pediatric, obstetric, surgical, and pharmacy review

FirstAid: Call Qatar 999 and do not self-drive. Do not give food, drink, laxatives, enemas, or pain medicines unless directed by an emergency clinician. Call Qatar 999 now, follow the call-taker's ambulance and emergency-transport instructions, and do not self-drive. Do not delay emergency care.
algorithm.Author: IST Health Open-Source Guideline Content
algorithm.LastRevised: RESEARCH_REQUIRED - internal IST clinical adaptation date is not recorded
algorithm.Copyright: Public-source content reused under its stated licence. This is not licensed STCC content.

questions.Question: Is nausea or vomiting the main concern rather than abdominal bloating or swelling?
questions.Information: Symptoms dominated by nausea or vomiting belong in the Nausea pathway.

questions.Question: Is there severe sudden or rapidly worsening abdominal pain, a rigid or very tender abdomen, vomiting blood, green vomit in a child, collapse, severe breathing difficulty, heavy bleeding, or pregnancy/postpartum with severe pain or faintness?
questions.Information: NHS.UK bloating guidance lists these as emergency-assessment criteria.

questions.Question: Is there bloating with persistent vomiting, diarrhea or constipation, pain, fever or chills, a lump, inability to pass urine/stool/gas, blood or black stool, weight loss, reduced child feeding or urine, possible pregnancy, recent surgery, immunocompromise, or a medicine-related concern?
questions.Information: NHS.UK guidance lists these as reasons for urgent clinical review.

questions.Question: For an otherwise well adult who is not pregnant or recently postpartum, is this mild short-lived bloating with none of the emergency, urgent, pediatric, or vulnerability features above?
questions.Information: NHS.UK guidance describes mild bloating as manageable at home with diet and lifestyle changes.

advice.Title: Emergency bloating precautions
Content: Call Qatar 999 and do not self-drive. Do not give food, drink, laxatives, enemas, or pain medicines unless directed by an emergency clinician. Call Qatar 999 now, follow the call-taker's ambulance and emergency-transport instructions, and do not self-drive. Do not delay emergency care.
Call Back If: worsening pain, rigidity, collapse, bleeding, or vomiting; worsening breathing difficulty.

advice.Title: Urgent bloating review
Content: Arrange same-day in-person assessment through the Qatar route approved for this UAT environment. Do not recommend a laxative, antacid, antiemetic, or other medicine until age, pregnancy, obstruction risk, comorbidity, allergies, and current medicines have been checked.
Call Back If: pain, vomiting, distension, or fever worsens; blood, black stool, inability to pass stool/gas/urine, faintness, or reduced responsiveness develops.

advice.Title: Home care for mild bloating
Content: Stay physically active, chew with your mouth closed to avoid swallowing air, drink enough water, eat smaller and more frequent meals, and gently massage the stomach from right to left. Avoid fizzy drinks, excess caffeine and alcohol, gas-producing foods, and large late meals.
Call Back If: pain, vomiting, or fever develops; does not improve with self-care.

searchwords: bloated and gassy for the past few days

initialAssessmentQuestions.Question: What is the patient's age and sex, when did swelling start, and is pregnancy possible or confirmed or has there been a recent delivery or abdominal procedure?
initialAssessmentQuestions.Rationale: Condition-relevant assessment retained from the cited Batch 17 source.

initialAssessmentQuestions.Question: What is the temperature, if measured, and is there severe or localized pain, breathing difficulty, faintness, a rigid abdomen, or rapidly increasing swelling?
initialAssessmentQuestions.Rationale: Condition-relevant assessment retained from the cited Batch 17 source.

initialAssessmentQuestions.Question: Is there green or bloody vomit, vomiting blood, blood or black stool, inability to pass stool/gas/urine, reduced feeding or wet diapers in a child, a lump, weight loss, immunocompromise, or medicines that may cause constipation?
initialAssessmentQuestions.Rationale: Condition-relevant assessment retained from the cited Batch 17 source.

initialAssessmentQuestions.Question: What has a safe parent or caregiver observed about alertness, breathing, pain, swelling, fever, eating or drinking, sleep, play, and normal activity?
initialAssessmentQuestions.Rationale: Child assessment adds safe-caregiver observations without inventing a different clinical threshold.
initialAssessmentQuestions.Source: IST pediatric telephone-assessment adaptation; governance review required
